en: Abhidhānottara 13 = Palm-leaf manuscript = Raghu Vīra’s manuscript reproduction by Lokesh Chandra
Now I shall explain another [method], the sequence of the ritual for the Yogavīras;
I shall declare the true nature of the Yoginī-pīṭhas and the oral tradition.
This is for all heroic yoginīs on the festivals of the gurus, and not otherwise;
it is the most beautiful oral tradition of all the ḍākinīs.
One should draw nine squares and so forth in the center, and outside of that, sixteen;
in the centers of the middle squares, one should draw a very beautiful lotus.
Having created there in the center an eight-petaled lotus with universal petals, a pericarp, and a mass of filaments, he should join [the letters] beginning with 'a' therein.
Then, having visualized the vowels and consonants likewise contained within the syllable HŪṂ,
one should meditate on the state of Heruka through the transformation of Vajrasattva.
Five-faced and ten-armed, adorned by Vārāhī,
with faces that are white, blue, red, green, and yellow, and with hair of the same colors.
Three-eyed, with a formidable face, well-established in the *ālīḍha* and *pratyālīḍha* postures,
[he is] Bhairava and Kālarātri, utterly overwhelmed and trampled underfoot.
Wearing a crown of garlands of skulls and bearing the half-moon, he is auspicious;
his crown is adorned with a double-vajra, and his matted locks form a formidable crest.
The body is sealed with the six mudrās, adorned with vajra ornaments,
joined in union with the vajra-bell, and is the supreme great bliss.
In the two fourth [hands], he holds a trident, a hand-drum, a vajra, a flaying-knife, a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, the head of Brahmā, and an axe.
With her left and right hands,
she likewise wraps a human skin garment around her two feet, and thus she is embraced by Vārāhī.
She has the same color, arms, and physical form [as the deity], with disheveled hair, naked,
wearing a tiger-skin garment, and a girdle adorned with fragments.
Wearing a garland of skulls, the fierce Raudrī is intensely overwhelmed by compassion and passion; on the eastern petal is Ḍākinī, on the north Lāmaḍākinī,
on the west Khaṇḍarohā, and on the south Rūpaḍākinī.
Black, dark green, red, and fair-complexioned, naked, and standing in the *ālīḍha* posture;
adorned with a crown of skulls, with disheveled hair, she shines resplendent.
In all the corner sections, there is a skull-cup containing the *bodhicitta*.
Holding a skull-cup, a khaṭvāṅga staff, a bell, a hand-drum, a flaying knife, and a severed head;
three-faced and three-eyed, she is adorned, fierce, red with passion, and agitated;
gazing at the face of the Blessed One, she is deeply enamored and full of great longing.
Wearing a garland of severed heads as a necklace, one should visualize that Heruka.
Thus, in the center, one should visualize that supreme square within it.
In the eastern squares of that very place, at Pullīramalaya, is Khaṇḍakapālin with Pracaṇḍā, who is yellow.
In the north, at Jālandhara, is Mahākaṅkāla and Caṇḍākṣī, who are blue;
in the west, at Oḍiyāna, is Kaṅkālaprabhāvatī, who is white;
in the south, at Arbuda, is Vikaṭadaṃṣṭrin and Mahānāsā, who are green.
In the southeast, at Godāvarī, Surāvairiṇī and Vīramatī are red;
in the southwest, at Rāmeśvara, Amitābha and Kharvarī are as pale as a lotus;
in the northwest, at Devikoṭa, Vajraprabhā and Laṅkeśvarī are smoke-blue.
In the northeast, in Mālava, there is Haritā, who has a body of vajra and the shade of a tree;
her hands hold a vajra-bell while embracing [her consort].
There, in the second square in the east, in Kāmarūpaka, is Aṅkurikā-Airāvatī, who is red.
In the north, in Oḍra, Vajrajaṭilāmahābhairavā is green;
in the west, in Triśakuni, Mahāvīravāyuvegā is blue;
in the south, in Kosala, Vajrahūṃkārasurābhakṣī is white.
In the southeast, at Kaliṅga, Subhadraśyāmādevī is sky-blue;
in the southwest, at Lampāka, Vajraprabhasubhadrā is red;
in the northwest, at Kāñcika, Mahābhairavahayakarṇā is yellow.
In the northeast, on the Himalaya, is Virūpākṣa; Khagānanā is blue, holding a lotus and embracing a bell.
In the third enclosure, in the east, in Pretapurī, are Mahābala and Cakravega; they are sky-blue.
In the north, at Gṛhadevatā, Ratnavajrakhaṇḍarohā is yellow.
In the west, at Saurāṣṭra, Hayagrīvaśauṇḍinī is red.
In the south, at Suvarṇadvīpa, Ākāśagarbhacakravarminī is blue.
In the city of Agneyī, Herukasuvīrā is smoke-colored;
in the Sindhu of Nairṛtī, Padmanarteśvaramahābalā is green;
in the Maru of Vāyavī, Vairocanacakravartinī is blue.
In the northeast, at Kulatā, is Vajrasattva Mahāvīryā, white in color, embracing a consort holding a wheel and a bell.

The others have six arms and three faces, and according to the sequence of the oral instructions, their faces are as follows: they hold a *khaṭvāṅga*, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a flaying knife (*kartikā*), and carry a severed head (*muṇḍa*). They stand in the *ālīḍha* posture, are adorned with the five mudrās, wear garments of tiger skin, are decorated with garlands of heads, and have crowns made of garlands of skulls. On their foreheads, a vajra, a lotus, and a wheel should be visualized in the proper sequence.
The goddesses have disheveled hair and are naked, their two shanks well-adorned;
as is the means (upāya), so is wisdom (prajñā), perfectly established with their characteristic mudrās.
